message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"12.1","text":"After leaving Tripolis in Phoenicia to make our way toward Antioch in Syria, we came to Orthosia and stayed there that same day. Because it was near the city we had left, and almost everyone there had already heard the proclamation, we stayed there one day and departed for Antaradus. Since many people were traveling with us, Peter spoke to Nicetas and Aquila, saying, “Because the large crowd of those traveling with us attracts no small amount of envy toward us as we enter each city, I have thought it necessary to consider how to ensure that neither these people are distressed by being prevented from staying with us nor we, by becoming conspicuous, fall prey to the envy born of malice. For this reason, I want you, Nicetas, and Aquila to go ahead of me separately, as two parties, each on his own, and to enter the Gentile cities.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Ἐκβάντες οὖν τὴν Τρίπολιν τῆς Φοινίκης ὡς ἐπὶ Ἀντιόχειαν τῆς Συρίας ἐλθεῖν","chosen":"After leaving Tripolis in Phoenicia to make our way toward Antioch in Syria","rationale":"The construction presents Antioch as the intended direction or destination of the journey, not as a place already reached."},{"source_quote":"προακηκοότων τοῦ κηρύγματος","chosen":"had already heard the proclamation","rationale":"The prefix προ- indicates prior hearing; κήρυγμα denotes the message proclaimed or the act of proclamation."},{"source_quote":"φθόνῳ τῷ τῆς κακίας","chosen":"the envy born of malice","rationale":"The genitive links the envy with κακία, which may denote malice or wickedness; “the envy of wickedness” is a more formally literal alternative."},{"source_quote":"κατὰ συστήματα δύο σποράδην μονωθέντας","chosen":"separately, as two parties, each on his own","rationale":"The wording depicts Nicetas and Aquila as divided into two units and isolated from the larger company. Alternatively, κατὰ συστήματα δύο could be understood as “in groups of two,” though the participle agrees with the two named men."},{"source_quote":"τὰς τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσέρχεσθαι πόλεις","chosen":"to enter the Gentile cities","rationale":"Here τὰ ἔθνη designates non-Jewish peoples; “cities of the nations” is a more literal alternative."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.2","text":"“I know that, now that you have heard this, you are disheartened about doing it, although you will be separated from me for an interval of not even two full days. I therefore want you to know that we who persuaded you love you who were persuaded many times more than you love us who persuaded you. Since we love one another, then, let us take thought for safety, as far as lies with us, by not irrationally doing whatever we want. Besides, you will not be away from me on any day when I am giving a discourse. For I have decided—as you yourselves know—to stay for days and discourse in the more prominent cities of the provinces. For now, go ahead to Laodicea, which is nearer to us, and after two or three days—as far as it depends on my own choice—I will catch up with you. Wait for me at the gates, you alone, because of the commotion, so that by entering together without noise we may be with you. From there, likewise, after we have stayed for days, others in your place should go ahead in daily rotation to the places beyond, preparing the lodgings.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀθυμεῖτε","chosen":"you are disheartened","rationale":"The verb expresses loss of heart or discouragement rather than simple sadness."},{"source_quote":"πολλαπλάσιον ἀγαπῶμεν","chosen":"love ... many times more","rationale":"πολλαπλάσιον gives a comparative idea of manifold or many-times-greater love."},{"source_quote":"τῷ μὴ ἀλόγως ποιεῖν ἃ θέλομεν","chosen":"by not irrationally doing whatever we want","rationale":"The articular infinitive is instrumental, explaining how they are to attend to their safety."},{"source_quote":"οὐδεμιᾶς ἡμέρας διαλεγομένου μου ἀπελιμπάνεσθε","chosen":"you will not be away from me on any day when I am giving a discourse","rationale":"The promise is that their brief advance journey will not cause them to miss a day on which Peter teaches."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὸν θρῦλον","chosen":"because of the commotion","rationale":"θρῦλος can denote noise, public stir, or widespread talk; the concern here is the attention created at the gates."},{"source_quote":"κατὰ ἐφημερίας","chosen":"in daily rotation","rationale":"The phrase indicates service or assignments apportioned by the day; “by daily turns” is an alternative."},{"source_quote":"τὰς ξενίας ἑτοιμάζοντες","chosen":"preparing the lodgings","rationale":"ξενία can denote hospitality or guest accommodation; the practical task here is arranging places to stay."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.3","text":"When Peter had said this, they were compelled to consent, saying, “It does not greatly distress us, lord, to do this, because we are commanded by you. First, being worthy, you were chosen by God’s providence to understand everything well and to give sound counsel. Besides, the necessity of going ahead separates us from you for at most two days. Even these are a long time when it comes to not seeing you, Peter our lord. Yet we reflect that those sent much farther ahead will be more distressed, since they have been commanded to wait longer for you in each city, grieving because they are deprived for a longer time of seeing your much-longed-for face. Although we are no less disheartened than they, we do not object to doing as you command, because it is beneficial.” After saying this together, they went ahead, having instructions to speak at the first inn to the crowd traveling with them, so that, after becoming dispersed from one another, they might enter the cities.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἠναγκάσθησαν συνθέσθαι","chosen":"they were compelled to consent","rationale":"συντίθεμαι here means agreeing to a proposal; the passive of ἀναγκάζω conveys their reluctant necessity."},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ ἡμερῶν δύο","chosen":"for at most two days","rationale":"In this context ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ is taken as marking an upper limit. “As a rule, for two days” is also grammatically possible."},{"source_quote":"πάντα καλῶς νοεῖν τε καὶ συμβουλεύειν","chosen":"to understand everything well and to give sound counsel","rationale":"πάντα is taken with the coordinated infinitives, while συμβουλεύειν denotes advising rather than merely deliberating privately."},{"source_quote":"οἱ πολὺ μακρὰν προπεμπόμενοι","chosen":"those sent much farther ahead","rationale":"προπέμπω here refers to dispatching people in advance, and πολὺ μακράν emphasizes the greater distance."},{"source_quote":"τὸ περιπόθητον πρόσωπον","chosen":"your much-longed-for face","rationale":"περιπόθητος expresses intense longing or dearness, and πρόσωπον retains the concrete image of the face."},{"source_quote":"ὁμῶς ταῦτα εἰπόντες προῆξαν","chosen":"After saying this together, they went ahead","rationale":"The selected edition prints ὁμῶς, whose accentuation supports “alike” or “together,” so the adverb is taken with the plural speakers. If the printed accentuation is an orthographic or editorial feature representing ὅμως, the contextual alternative is “Nevertheless, after saying this, they went ahead.”"},{"source_quote":"σποράδην ἀλλήλων γενόμενοι","chosen":"after becoming dispersed from one another","rationale":"The adverb depicts the travelers becoming scattered rather than entering as an organized mass."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὁμῶς ταῦτα εἰπόντες προῆξαν","issue":"The image-checked selected edition prints ὁμῶς, not the normally adversative ὅμως. The translation follows the printed accentuation with “together.” Context could support “nevertheless” if the accentuation is an editorial or orthographic feature, but the supplied Greek has not been altered.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.4","text":"So, after they had gone, I, Clement, was exceedingly glad that he had told me to remain with him. I answered, “I thank God that you did not send me away as you did my companions, since I would have died in anguish.” But he said, “What, then? If there should also be some need for you to be sent somewhere for the sake of instruction, will you die just because, for your benefit, you are separated from me for a short time? Would you not instead, after talking it over with yourself, cheerfully undertake to bear what has been commanded of you because necessity required it? Or do you not know that friends are always together in their memories, even if they are separated in body, while some who are together in body are, because of forgetfulness, far away in soul from their friends?”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐπειδὴ ὀδυνώμενος ἂν διαπεφωνήκειν","chosen":"since I would have died in anguish","rationale":"In this context διαφωνέω carries the sense of failing, perishing, or dying, rather than making an outcry. Peter’s immediately following question, διὰ τοῦτο τεθνήξει, confirms the reference to death. The pluperfect with ἄν expresses the unreal result; “I would have perished in pain” is a close alternative."},{"source_quote":"μαθημάτων χάριν","chosen":"for the sake of instruction","rationale":"μαθήματα can concern lessons, learning, or teaching; the Greek does not specify whether Clement would primarily receive or provide the instruction."},{"source_quote":"συμφερόντως","chosen":"for your benefit","rationale":"The adverb indicates that the temporary separation serves an advantageous or expedient purpose."},{"source_quote":"προσομιλήσας σεαυτῷ","chosen":"after talking it over with yourself","rationale":"The phrase literally describes conversing with oneself and contextually implies inward reasoning or self-exhortation."},{"source_quote":"σύνεισιν αἰεὶ οἱ φίλοι ταῖς μνήμαις","chosen":"friends are always together in their memories","rationale":"The dative presents memories as the sphere or means by which absent friends remain together."},{"source_quote":"τὰς ψυχὰς ἀποδημοῦσιν τοῖς φίλοις","chosen":"are ... far away in soul from their friends","rationale":"The accusative marks respect—“as to their souls”—while ἀποδημέω preserves the image of being away from home."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"πορευθέντων· οὖν αὐτῶν","issue":"The selected edition prints a raised point between πορευθέντων and οὖν, interrupting the expected genitive-absolute word sequence. The translation treats the surviving words as the continuous construction “So, after they had gone,” without changing any Greek letters.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.5","text":"And I answered, “Do not suppose, then, my lord, that my distress would have been irrational; rather, it would have rested on entirely sound reasoning. For since I have you, my lord, in place of everyone—father, mother, brothers, and relatives—you who, for God’s sake, became for me the cause of the truth that saves, I receive the greatest consolation by having you in place of everyone. Moreover, fearing the desire natural to my youthful prime, I was anxious whether, if separated from you, young man that I am, I would be weaker than desire. On this point I now have such resistance that it would be impossible for me to leave you even under some wrath from God. But since it is far better and safer for me to be with you, the one whom my mind has rightly determined beforehand to revere, I therefore pray to be with you always. Furthermore, I remember you saying in Caesarea, ‘If anyone wishes to accompany me, let him accompany me reverently.’ By ‘reverently,’ you said you meant causing no one grief in matters relating to God—for example, by leaving behind parents, a like-minded wife, or any companions devoted to reverence for God. Thus I am in every respect a suitable traveling companion for you. Even if you grant me the greatest favors, you still permit me to perform the duties of servants.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰ λύπης πάσχειν ἤμελλον ἀνοήτως","chosen":"my distress would have been irrational","rationale":"Literally, Clement speaks of “suffering the things of sorrow”; the rendering expresses the claim in natural English without reducing λύπη to physical pain."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὸν θεὸν","chosen":"for God’s sake","rationale":"διά with the accusative is causal here. “Because of God” is more literal; “through God” would normally require the genitive."},{"source_quote":"τῆς σωζούσης ἀληθείας","chosen":"the truth that saves","rationale":"The participle directly characterizes the truth as saving and should not be reduced to merely helpful or correct teaching."},{"source_quote":"τῆς ἀκμῆς τὴν ἐκ φύσεως ἐπιθυμίαν","chosen":"the desire natural to my youthful prime","rationale":"ἀκμή denotes one’s prime or youthful vigor, while ἐκ φύσεως presents the desire as natural to that stage of life."},{"source_quote":"ἠγωνίων μήπως ἀπολειφθείς σου, ἄνθρωπος ὢν νεώτερος","chosen":"I was anxious whether, if separated from you, young man that I am","rationale":"The participles describe the circumstance feared by Clement. The final εἰ-clause is taken as resuming and completing this expression of anxiety."},{"source_quote":"ἀποστῆναί σου ἀδύνατον","chosen":"it would be impossible for me to leave you","rationale":"The infinitive immediately precedes ἀδύνατον and is taken as its complement. This keeps Clement’s inability to leave Peter distinct from his earlier fear about what might happen if Peter left him behind."},{"source_quote":"εἰ ἥττων ἐπιθυμίας ἔσομαι","chosen":"whether ... I would be weaker than desire","rationale":"The clause is taken once, as completing ἠγωνίων μήπως, rather than both completing the earlier anxiety and supplying a second assertion that such weakness is impossible."},{"source_quote":"ὁ νοῦς μου αἰδεῖσθαι εὐλόγως προείληφεν","chosen":"whom my mind has rightly determined beforehand to revere","rationale":"προλαμβάνω here indicates a prior resolve or settled choice, and αἰδεῖσθαι conveys reverence or respectful regard."},{"source_quote":"μηδένα λυπεῖν κατὰ θεόν","chosen":"causing no one grief in matters relating to God","rationale":"κατὰ θεόν can mean “in relation to God,” “according to God,” or “in a godly matter.” The examples concern obligations to people connected with devotion to God."},{"source_quote":"γυναῖκα ὁμόφρονα","chosen":"a like-minded wife","rationale":"ὁμόφρων describes one who shares the same outlook or purpose, here likely including religious commitment."},{"source_quote":"τὰς δούλων μοι ὑπηρεσίας συγχωρεῖς ποιεῖν","chosen":"you ... permit me to perform the duties of servants","rationale":"The phrase denotes subordinate personal service. “Slaves’ services” would make the bonded-status nuance more explicit, while “servants” follows the supplied wording policy."},{"source_quote":"εἰ καὶ τὰ μέγιστα χαρίζῃ","chosen":"Even if you grant me the greatest favors","rationale":"εἰ καί is read concessively. Alternatively, the permission to serve may itself be presented as one of the greatest favors, though that relationship is not syntactically explicit."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἠγωνίων μήπως ἀπολειφθείς σου, ἄνθρωπος ὢν νεώτερος, ὅπερ νῦν οὕτως ἐνστάσεως ἔχω, κἂν κατὰ τινὰ χόλον θεοῦ ἀποστῆναί σου ἀδύνατον εἰ ἥττων ἐπιθυμίας ἔσομαι","issue":"The verified wording is syntactically compressed, especially in the attachments of ὅπερ, ἐνστάσεως, κἄν, ἀδύνατον, and the final εἰ-clause. The translation takes ὅπερ resumptively as “on this point,” οὕτως ἐνστάσεως ἔχω as expressing strong resistance, ἀποστῆναί σου as the complement of ἀδύνατον, and εἰ ἥττων ἐπιθυμίας ἔσομαι as resuming ἠγωνίων μήπως. This avoids using the final clause twice. Alternatively, ὅπερ may refer specifically to the natural desire or to the entire feared circumstance, while οὕτως ... κἄν may be taken as a result construction under which being weaker than desire is declared impossible. That alternative leaves the immediately preceding ἀποστῆναί σου less naturally attached. No alteration of the selected Greek is proposed.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
